Biodiversity Strategy

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Biodiversity is big business - a strategy to monetise South Africa's wildlife and plants has divided conservation scientists.

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa's natural assets ..not just to be admired…but to be more aggressively exploited - for both money and jobs. That’s the Government’s vision for a transformed biodiversity economy - to harness our natural wealth like never before.


Summary:
The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment ( DFFE ) recently released a 48 page plan on its revised draft National Biodiversity Economy Strategy, which has proved to be extremely controversial among conservationists. The plan was aired at an indaba in Johannesburg in March, where President Cyril Ramaphosa addressed potential investors in the biodiversity economy. He said “lying hidden, like Rembrandts in the attic, are the endowments our people should now utilise – the land, the plants and everything else”. He emphasised the need to empower rural communities, and placed them at the centre of plans to radically transform the biodiversity economy.

The plan essentially aims to create mega living conservation landscapes – an increase from 20 million to 34 million hectares by 2040, to attract international trophy hunters, tourists, and investors from abroad. Environmental NGOs are sounding the alarm, and claim that South Africa will become the pariah of the conservation world if this plan is implemented. The plan essentially seeks to create jobs and increase revenue, focussing on rural communities benefitting from the commodification of a wide range of wildlife. This will include an increase in hunting, the slaughter of wild animals as a source of cheaper protein for rural communities, as well as the sale of rhino horn for medicinal purposes to Asian tourists. The domestic trade in ivory will also be stimulated, with ivory being available for purchase by tourists and investors.

The plans are ambitious.They include increasing areas under conservation from 20 million hectares to 34 million hectares. And increasing the number of international hunters annually.


Further information:
The story will focus on two opposing views. Pete Ruinard, who managed the Ithala game reserve in KZN for many years, is opposed to the plan. He doesn't believe our government will be able to effectively implement it. He believes an increase in fair chase trophy hunting will also be a disaster for Brand South Africa. Dr Haylyey Clements, from the Wildlife Economy Institute, believes its the right way to go. She believes rural communities will benefit and there will be more jobs created. She believes its a move away from "fortress conservation" and is a strategy that is heading in the right direction.

0000-00-00

Script:


NATSOUND of male lions roaring

VO 1 Imagine biodiversity as a massive treasure chest…filled with incredible animals, plants, and marine life.

VO 2 A biodiversity economy finds creative ways to use those treasures…and at the same time conserve them.

VO 3 Activities that include safaris…recreational hunting and wild meat harvesting… using plants for medicinal purposes…to generate both money and jobs.

VO 4 Government has clung to this strategy for years…but brace yourself…fresh plans to radically ramp it up on a massive scale were unveiled by the President in March.

UPSOUND Cyril Ramaphosa 00:31:14:26 “Lying hidden like Rembrandts or Gerard Sekoto pieces lying in the attic are the endowments that our people should now utilise - the land, the plants, and everything else that is in our rural communities.”(Biodiversity Economy and Investment Indaba / March 26, 2024) (whatsapped youtube clip)

VO 5 But, are government’s plans too ambitious? Does the strategy, as some say, have potentially devastating consequences?

CUT TO BLACK

VO 6 Dr Hayley Clements is a senior researcher at Stellenbosch University’s African Wildlife Economy Institute. And she is a firm believer in government’s plan.

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements / Stellenbosch University Senior researcher (Day 1 / Clip 0001) 05:24 The strategy actually has been in place since 2016. And I think one of the main reasons for this revision is to bring it more in line with international commitments.

VO 7 The global biodiversity framework is a new international agreement in which all participating countries have to conserve 30% of their land by 2030. Our government has come up with a strategy to attempt to achieve this.

LINK The government’s revised strategy was released as a 48 page document in March…the public was given only two weeks to comment, extended by a further two weeks, after an outcry…

VO 8 Some environmental organisations were shocked by the scale of the vision like wanting to increase revenue from all types of hunting from 4.6 billion to 27.6 billion by 2036. This includes trophy hunting - a sport that typically targets the strongest, most dominant of a species.

VO 9 Trophy hunting ruffles feathers. Dr Ross Harvey, director of research at Good Governance Africa, thinks that’s for good reason…. As South Africa runs the risk of ethically minded tourists boycotting the country.

UPSOUND Dr Ross Harvey / Good Governance Africa Time code 10:40 You don’t know as a tourist whether that elephant that you’re taking a photograph of today is still going to be here tomorrow. And people are not willing to live with that cognitive dissonance any longer.

LINK Clip 0082 / Day 2 The trophy hunting industry contributes significantly to our economy and it creates jobs. But, how does that money find its way back to conservation?

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements ( Day 1 / Clip 0001) Time code 04:03 If its managed well its actually just harvesting a very small percentage of a wildlfe population that actually brings in a lot of revenue for conservation particularly in areas where eco tourism is not very viable.

VO 10 Ross disagrees, and says just a fraction of the money made from trophy hunting goes back into conservation.

UPSOUND Dr Ross Harvey “The portion of cash that goes back into conservation from selling the licences to the trophy hunter of any kind of species is minimal. So this idea that hunting will generate all kinds of cash that comes at little ecological cost, that’s a misnomer.

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements “I think a lot of the uproar is about trophy hunting but that’s only one tool in a big toolbox. There’s a big focus on eco-tourism in this strategy. There’s a focus on hunting for meat which I think is something that morally people tend to be less opposed to, there’s also a focus on bio-prospecting, harvesting of wild plants etc. So it would not be wise to focus the whole strategy on trophy hunting and that’s certainly not what it does.

VO 11 On the other hand, their plan to expand conservation areas from 20 million hectares to 34 million hectares by 2040 has been welcomed by many.

LINK Clip 0079 / Day Two The commercialisation of our biodiversity could, according to government, benefit rural communities. And that would be great, but the question is, is the plan ecologically sustainable?

VO 12 Hayley is confident the strategy will do just that.

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements “And so it’s saying if we give people opportunity to utilise biodiversity in sustainable ways then they will be incentivised to conserve it.

VO 13 Government’s strategy places rural communities at its centre.

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements: The wildlife economy so far has primarily occurred on white farmland. And the government recognises and rightly so that there is really a need to grow this industry through better inclusion of emerging black farmers as well as communities that hold land.

VO 14 But she emphasises it will be up to communities not to exploit what they have.

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements The idea is if they don’t manage it sustainably then they won’t have a livelihood going forward.

VO 15 That’s not a risk Pete Ruinard thinks we should take if we are serious about conservation.

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard / Private Nature Reserve Manager “I think we are playing a game with something here that is irreplaceable.

VO 16 Pete is an environmental manager, and dedicated thirty years of his life to managing state-owned game reserves in Kwazulu-Natal.

VO 17 Two years ago, he left KZN conservation, exchanging it for the stark beauty of the West Coast where he now manages a private nature reserve.

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard “I think there should rather be a focus on look this is what we’ve got, let’s fix that up first before we start considering these very ambitious, broad plans. It is really incumbent on the government, and this is at both provincial level and national level to better financially resource these agencies, because that’s the only way it’s going to start to turn around.

VO 18 Many provincial game reserves are in a state of near collapse. This new plan places oversight in the hands of provincial conservation authorities… but, if they’re already battling, how will they be able to implement it?

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard / Private Nature Reserve Manager “There’s really one extremely important pillar that the entire possible success of this strategy rests on and that is the concept of good governance.

MASA: And that is not something we have in abundant supply.

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard “No, the provincial conservation agencies are under severe stress. You’re placing a huge burden on an organisation that is already struggling just to maintain what they’re dealing with now.”

VO 19 Pete is also caught up on the part of the plan that seeks to increase trophy hunting.

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard “When your trophy bull of whatever it is has been shot it’s gone. You’re taking that same genetic virility that’s so important for the survival of that specific species in a given environment and you’re taking it out of the system. So you’re not doing anybody any ecological favours through trophy hunting.

NATSOUND FROM BLOOD LIONS DOCCIE “This stuff will be gone before we even know it and its much more important than we think”.

VO 20 In 2015, Ian Michler, director of the documentary Blood Lions, exposed what was happening with canned hunting on lion breeding farms. And while government recently announced their intention to shut down that industry, Ian believes we have a long way to go. And that trophy hunting should be banned outright.

UPSOUND Ian Michler / Director: Blood Lions “I don’t like the pure instrumental value approach to the way this government and others in Southern Africa carry out their conservation objectives. Wildlife or biodiversity and protected areas in their eyes only has value in terms of its benefits to humanity.

NATSOUND From DOCCIE

VO 21 And viewing it through that lens, he believes, could have a catastrophic impact.

UPSOUND Ian Michler / Director: Blood Lions “We’re going to end up farming high value wildlife species like buffalo, sable, lion, rhino, and that’s got nothing to do with biodiversity conservation. It’s merely switching from farming domestic animals to farming wild animals and by the way if this process goes on for 20, 30 years then we are on the road to domesticating these very species we hold so dear and wild to us.

LINK Clip 0087 / Day 2 The international trade of rhino horn or elephant ivory is currently restricted. But, government wants to explore options of domestic trade.

VO 22 Government wants to create health clinics and sell rhino horn to tourists from the Far East…another controversial aspect of this strategy.

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard Clip 0029 Time code 20:18 you now placing a legal pressure on the resource combined with the continuing illegal pressure on the resource, and those two combined are obviously going to place more pressure on the species.

MASA (asking Hayley) What do you make of the plans of selling powdered rhino horn to Asian tourists?

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements “So the evidence suggests that if you allow people to utilise a species they see value in it, those populations grow. What’s happened since, of course because of poaching, is now its extremely costly for the state and for the private sector to protect those rhinos from poaching. And so something’s got to give. But, the reality is we need additional tools to save the white rhino.

VO 23 For Hayley, finding creative solutions that benefit BOTH people and conservation is what this strategy seeks to achieve, and if it works it could have benefits for generations to come.

UPSOUND Dr Hayley Clements “I actually think its the opposite of being detrimental to biodiversity. I think its trying to promote biodiversity conservation across the landscape.

VO 24 For Pete, there’s simply too much at stake.

UPSOUND Pete Ruinard “If this kind of strategy goes ahead full steam, you actually run the risk of overexploitation and that overexploitation is going to damage Brand South Africa because our wildlife and our biodiversity they are our country’s heritage.
